items.prompt: The web tier scales on requests while a worker tier scales on queue age. Which configuration preserves independent behavior?
constraints: The tiers have different demand signals.
Each tier has its own capacity bounds.
A web spike should not launch workers without queued work.

options.text: Use separate Auto Scaling groups and policies with tier-specific metrics, bounds, warm-up, and health checks.
Put both tiers in one group and scale the group on the average of requests and queue age.
Scale workers whenever web CPU rises because all application work is equivalent.
Use one fixed capacity for both tiers so the policies cannot disagree.

feedback.Reason: Different components should scale against the signal that represents their own workload.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Separate groups let desired capacity, instance type, health, and scaling policy follow the tier's demand and lifecycle.
Details.scenarioApplication: Web request volume changes web capacity, while queue age changes worker capacity and downstream quotas remain protected.
Details.errorCorrection: Averaging unrelated signals hides bottlenecks, web CPU does not prove queued work, and fixed capacity removes elasticity.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: More groups add operational surface, but they prevent cross-tier overprovisioning and incorrect scale actions.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A shared average is not a meaningful demand signal for both workloads.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Web CPU does not establish worker backlog or processing capacity.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Fixed capacity cannot respond to independent workload changes.

items.prompt: A service needs to keep average request count per target near a chosen value. Which policy is the clearest fit?
constraints: The metric is published per target.
More targets reduce request load per target.
The service has defined minimum and maximum capacity.

options.text: Use target tracking on the per-target request metric, with bounds and warm-up tuned from measured service behavior.
Use a step policy based only on calendar time, regardless of request volume.
Scale in when the per-target request count rises above the target.
Use a database storage metric because every application request creates the same amount of storage.

feedback.Reason: Target tracking directly expresses a desired level for a demand metric that decreases as targets are added.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: The policy adjusts desired capacity toward the target while respecting group bounds and lifecycle behavior.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team confirms request count correlates with latency and verifies that the metric is valid during errors and partial outages.
Details.errorCorrection: Calendar-only scaling ignores actual demand, high request count should not trigger scale-in, and storage is not request capacity.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Target tracking can lag rapid changes, so minimum headroom and service-level alarms remain important.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Time alone does not represent the current request load.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: High request count per target indicates more capacity is needed, not less.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Storage growth is not a reliable proxy for request concurrency.

items.prompt: A workload has distinct operating regions: one instance is sufficient at normal load, four are needed at high load, and the transitions are known. Which approach may fit?
constraints: The metric thresholds are measured.
The workload has distinct capacity steps.
The policy must include cooldown and bounds.

options.text: Use a step-scaling policy with measured thresholds and adjustments, then validate hysteresis, warm-up, and downstream capacity.
Add one instance for every metric datapoint even when the metric remains above the same threshold.
Scale in at every threshold crossing because the workload has discrete steps.
Remove minimum and maximum limits so the policy can always follow the metric.

feedback.Reason: Step scaling can map measured threshold ranges to discrete capacity adjustments.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: A step policy changes capacity according to the breach magnitude and can be bounded and stabilized.
Details.scenarioApplication: Load tests verify each threshold, avoid repeated additions for one alarm period, and include instance readiness and dependency limits.
Details.errorCorrection: Per-datapoint additions cause runaway growth, threshold breaches can require scale-out, and unbounded groups remove safety controls.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Step policies require careful threshold and stabilization tuning; target tracking may be simpler when a stable target exists.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Repeated additions for the same condition can overshoot capacity.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: A high threshold breach generally indicates more capacity is needed, not scale-in.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Bounds protect cost, quotas, and downstream dependencies.

items.prompt: A worker group can scale rapidly but a downstream API allows only a fixed request rate. Which Auto Scaling setting is a necessary guardrail?
constraints: The downstream rate limit is finite.
The queue can absorb work temporarily.
The worker group must not exceed tested concurrency.

options.text: Set a maximum capacity and per-worker concurrency or rate limit aligned with downstream quota, then scale on queue age or backlog.
Set maximum capacity to the number of messages in the queue regardless of downstream quota.
Remove the maximum because the queue is durable and can hide every downstream overload.
Increase worker retries without delay so more workers can overcome throttling.

feedback.Reason: Capacity bounds and concurrency controls prevent a worker fleet from converting backlog into downstream overload.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: A maximum and rate limit shape the request rate while queue age remains a useful demand signal for adding bounded capacity.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team tests worker count against downstream quota, monitors queue age and throttles, and uses delayed retries for transient failures.
Details.errorCorrection: Queue length alone can exceed downstream capacity, removing the maximum creates runaway cost or throttling, and immediate retries amplify load.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A bounded worker fleet may increase queue latency, so the product must define freshness and backlog objectives.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Backlog size does not override a finite downstream rate limit.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: A durable queue stores work but does not make downstream overload safe.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Immediate retries create a retry storm and consume more downstream quota.

items.prompt: An application fleet needs a patched AMI and a new instance profile. Which change keeps future scale-out consistent?
constraints: New instances must use the patched image.
The fleet should be reproducible.
Existing instances require a controlled replacement plan.

options.text: Publish a new launch-template version, make it the group source for new capacity, and use an instance-refresh or rolling replacement strategy with health validation.
Patch each running instance manually and leave the launch configuration unchanged.
Change only the load balancer target group because target registration installs the AMI.
Wait for the next failure so Auto Scaling eventually discovers the new image automatically.

feedback.Reason: A versioned launch template makes replacement and future scale-out use an explicit, repeatable configuration.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: The group launches new instances from the selected template version; controlled refresh replaces old instances while respecting health and availability.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team tests the new image, updates the group, refreshes in batches, and verifies target health before proceeding.
Details.errorCorrection: Manual patches drift, target groups do not install images, and failures should not be the deployment mechanism.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Refreshes consume capacity and may require surge or minimum-healthy settings, so rollout needs a recovery plan.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Manual drift means future replacements still use the old configuration.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Target registration routes traffic and does not define instance image or identity.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Waiting for failure creates an uncontrolled and inconsistent rollout.

items.prompt: Instances pass EC2 status checks but return HTTP 500 for every request. Which health-check choice improves fleet behavior?
constraints: The load balancer can observe application health.
An unhealthy application target should not receive requests.
Replacement must not create a loop for a shared dependency failure.

options.text: Use an application-aware load-balancer health check and configure Auto Scaling replacement only with a health endpoint that represents usable service capacity.
Use only EC2 status checks because an operating instance is always a healthy application target.
Return HTTP 200 from the health endpoint without checking dependencies so every target stays in service.
Disable health checks because replacement causes unnecessary instance launches.

feedback.Reason: Infrastructure health and application readiness are different signals; routing should reflect the service contract.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Load-balancer health checks can test an application endpoint and Auto Scaling can replace instances deemed unhealthy, subject to dependency-aware design.
Details.scenarioApplication: The endpoint checks critical local readiness without making every shared dependency outage look like every instance is independently broken.
Details.errorCorrection: EC2 status does not prove HTTP health, unconditional 200 hides failure, and disabling checks routes to unusable targets.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Deep dependency checks can cause replacement storms, so the health contract must distinguish local readiness from shared outage.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: An instance can be running while its application is failing.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: A health endpoint that always returns success defeats health-based routing.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Without health checks, failed capacity remains in service.

items.prompt: A new application version must roll through a fleet without taking all targets out of service. Which release mechanism should be evaluated?
constraints: The fleet has a minimum healthy capacity.
The new version can be tested on a subset.
Rollback must be possible.

options.text: Use a controlled rolling or instance-refresh deployment with minimum healthy and surge settings, target health validation, and a rollback decision.
Terminate the entire fleet and launch the new version simultaneously because parallel replacement is always fastest for users.
Change the image tag in the registry and assume running instances update themselves safely.
Deploy the new version to one instance and route all traffic there before testing it.

feedback.Reason: Controlled replacement preserves capacity while the new version proves its health and behavior.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: A refresh can replace instances in batches and use health checks and minimum healthy capacity to constrain risk.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team can pause or roll back after observing errors, latency, and dependency behavior on the new instances.
Details.errorCorrection: Fleet-wide termination creates an outage, running instances do not change from a registry tag alone, and one untested target is a single failure boundary.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A safer rollout may take longer and need surge capacity, but it reduces blast radius.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Replacing all capacity at once creates a large outage and rollback boundary.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Running instances do not automatically reload an image tag without a deployment action.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Sending all traffic to one untested instance removes resilience and increases release risk.

items.prompt: An instance must upload buffered events before termination. Which lifecycle control is appropriate?
constraints: Buffered events have a durable destination.
Termination must not discard acknowledged work.
The hook cannot block forever.

options.text: Use a lifecycle hook or graceful-drain path to stop new work, flush or release buffered events, complete within a bound, and then continue termination.
Terminate immediately because Auto Scaling cannot coordinate application shutdown.
Acknowledge events before they are uploaded so termination sees no pending work.
Keep the instance indefinitely and disable scale-in after the first buffered event.

feedback.Reason: Lifecycle coordination gives the application a bounded opportunity to preserve or release work before capacity is removed.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: A hook pauses the lifecycle transition while the application drains, uploads, or returns work to a durable queue.
Details.scenarioApplication: The drain path has a timeout and monitoring so a stuck instance does not block scaling forever.
Details.errorCorrection: Immediate termination can lose buffers, early acknowledgment hides incomplete work, and permanent capacity defeats scale-in.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Drain time delays scale-in, so the maximum and recovery behavior must be chosen from the work contract.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Application work can be interrupted or lost without lifecycle coordination.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Acknowledging before durable upload removes the work from retry visibility.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: A single buffered event should not disable fleet elasticity indefinitely.

items.prompt: A workload has large but predictable morning bursts and instances take several minutes to initialize. Which capacity feature may reduce response delay?
constraints: Initialization is expensive.
The workload can keep stopped or warm capacity ready.
Cost must be compared with the latency objective.

options.text: Evaluate a warm-pool or scheduled-capacity strategy, measure its cost and readiness benefit, and retain reactive scaling for forecast error.
Remove initialization steps from the image without testing whether the application still has required data and dependencies.
Scale only after the burst has ended because startup no longer affects demand then.
Keep the maximum number of fully active instances at all times regardless of demand.

feedback.Reason: Preinitialized capacity can reduce launch latency when startup is a material part of the service objective.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Warm capacity separates expensive initialization from the moment the service needs to add serving targets.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team measures readiness, refreshes warm images safely, and compares idle cost with the value of meeting the morning latency target.
Details.errorCorrection: Removing required initialization risks correctness, post-burst scale is too late, and permanent maximum capacity wastes cost.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Warm capacity costs resources and needs refresh and security maintenance, so it should be justified by measured startup and demand.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Skipping required initialization can create unhealthy or incorrect targets.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Capacity that arrives after demand cannot protect the burst objective.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Keeping maximum active capacity ignores elasticity and cost requirements.

items.prompt: A fleet has flexible workers and wants capacity across more than one EC2 instance type. Which design should be evaluated?
constraints: Workers tolerate different compatible instance types.
Capacity availability can vary by type.
The group must preserve workload and cost requirements.

options.text: Use a launch template and mixed-instances policy with explicit weighting, purchase options, capacity limits, and workload compatibility tests.
Mix arbitrary instance types without weighting because one instance always represents the same capacity.
Use only the largest type because variety prevents Auto Scaling from making a decision.
Allow instances with incompatible architecture because workers can always translate binaries at runtime.

feedback.Reason: Mixed capacity can improve availability or cost only when capacity units and workload compatibility are explicit.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: A mixed policy can select among compatible types and use weights or allocation behavior to represent different capacity contributions.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team tests CPU, memory, network, architecture, startup, and licensing constraints before using a mixed group.
Details.errorCorrection: Unweighted types can misrepresent capacity, largest-only forfeits flexibility, and incompatible binaries do not become portable automatically.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: More instance options complicate testing and observability, so the allowed set should remain intentional.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Different types can provide different capacity and must be represented correctly.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Using one largest type can increase cost and reduce availability options.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Architecture incompatibility is a runtime constraint, not something Auto Scaling translates.

items.prompt: A fault-tolerant batch worker can be interrupted and retry its job. Which capacity option may reduce cost?
constraints: Work is checkpointed or retryable.
The application tolerates interruption.
A durable queue or scheduler can replace capacity.

options.text: Evaluate Spot capacity for the worker group with interruption handling, queue visibility, idempotent jobs, and sufficient on-demand or other fallback capacity.
Use Spot for the only interactive production target whose requests cannot be retried.
Acknowledge every job immediately so an interruption cannot return it to the queue.
Ignore interruption notices because Auto Scaling guarantees a Spot instance will finish its process.

feedback.Reason: Spot is appropriate only when the workload and recovery design tolerate interruption.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Interruption-aware workers can release or retry work while a mixed or fallback capacity plan preserves progress.
Details.scenarioApplication: The worker stops accepting work, extends or releases visibility as appropriate, and another target completes the idempotent unit.
Details.errorCorrection: Non-retryable interactive work is a poor fit, early acknowledgment loses work, and Spot interruption can occur before completion.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Spot improves cost but introduces interruption and capacity uncertainty that must be reflected in queue age and service objectives.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A non-retryable interactive target cannot safely absorb interruption.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Early acknowledgment removes the work from reliable recovery visibility.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Auto Scaling replaces capacity but cannot guarantee an interrupted process completes.

items.prompt: A worker has claimed a non-idempotent job and cannot safely be interrupted until a commit is complete. What should scale-in do?
constraints: The job has a commit boundary.
Duplicate processing is unsafe.
Work can be delayed until the commit or released safely.

options.text: Protect or drain the worker through the commit boundary, then terminate it only after the job is complete or a safe recovery path has released ownership.
Terminate the worker immediately because scale-in has priority over job correctness.
Copy the process memory to another worker without an application checkpoint.
Acknowledge the job at claim time so the system will not retry it.

feedback.Reason: Scale-in must respect the work's correctness boundary and coordinate termination with ownership.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Protection and draining keep a claimed job from being interrupted, while a bounded recovery path handles workers that do not complete.
Details.scenarioApplication: The worker reports progress and the queue or coordinator knows when ownership can be retried safely.
Details.errorCorrection: Immediate termination can corrupt work, memory copying is not a durable checkpoint, and early acknowledgment hides unfinished work.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Protection can delay cost reduction, so jobs need maximum duration and recovery rules.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Capacity savings do not justify breaking a non-idempotent commit.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Process memory is not a portable durable checkpoint.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Acknowledging before commit removes the job from recovery despite incomplete work.

items.prompt: A web fleet must survive an Availability Zone failure while scaling. Which group configuration supports the requirement?
constraints: The load balancer spans multiple Availability Zones.
The fleet must not place all capacity in one zone.
The group should rebalance after capacity changes.

options.text: Configure the Auto Scaling group across multiple Availability Zones and subnets, use balanced distribution or rebalancing behavior, and verify target health per zone.
Use one large instance in one Availability Zone because vertical capacity replaces failure-domain diversity.
Place all instances in the zone with the lowest current price regardless of failure risk.
Use DNS round robin without health or zone-aware capacity controls.

feedback.Reason: Multi-AZ capacity and distribution reduce the chance that one zone failure removes the whole serving fleet.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: The group can launch and replace instances across selected subnets, while the load balancer routes only to healthy targets.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team tests zone loss, checks remaining capacity against the service objective, and prevents a scale action from concentrating all instances.
Details.errorCorrection: One large host and one zone preserve a single failure domain, price-only placement ignores availability, and DNS alone lacks target health semantics.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Multi-AZ capacity costs more coordination and may affect subnet or quota planning, but supports fault isolation.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Vertical capacity does not remove the Availability Zone failure domain.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Lowest price is not sufficient evidence for availability placement.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: DNS round robin does not provide the same health-aware target and capacity behavior.

items.prompt: Two scaling policies can request different desired capacities for the same group. What should the architect verify?
constraints: The policies use different signals.
The group has a bounded capacity range.
Unexpected policy interaction can cause oscillation or cost growth.

options.text: Understand policy precedence and interaction, choose complementary signals, and test the combined behavior against group bounds and service objectives.
Add as many policies as possible because more alarms always improve scaling accuracy.
Ignore policy interaction because Auto Scaling applies every request independently without a final desired capacity.
Remove the group maximum so competing policies can always reach their requested capacity.

feedback.Reason: Multiple policies can interact, so their semantics and combined capacity behavior must be tested rather than assumed.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Policies contribute desired-capacity decisions within group limits; incompatible signals can cause oscillation or unnecessary scale-out.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team selects signals with clear ownership and observes desired, running, healthy, and serving capacity under combined load.
Details.errorCorrection: Policy count is not accuracy, the group does converge on a capacity decision, and removing maximum removes a safety boundary.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: More signals can improve coverage but increase tuning and diagnosis complexity.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Unrelated or noisy policies can conflict and increase instability.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Policy interaction affects desired capacity and must be understood.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: A maximum protects cost, quotas, and downstream systems.

items.prompt: A service requires two healthy targets in each of two Availability Zones even during normal operation. Which group setting is part of the design?
constraints: The service has a minimum healthy capacity.
Two zones are required for the failure objective.
Scale-in must not remove required baseline capacity.

options.text: Set a tested minimum capacity and distribution across the required subnets, then ensure scale-in and health behavior preserve the baseline.
Set minimum capacity to one because Auto Scaling can create the other targets only after a zone fails.
Use maximum capacity as the only availability control and permit minimum capacity to reach zero.
Place two interfaces on one instance because network interfaces equal independent targets.

feedback.Reason: The minimum and placement policy must preserve the baseline capacity required by the availability objective.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Group bounds and subnet distribution control how much healthy capacity exists before a demand alarm or failure event.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team simulates an instance and zone loss and confirms the remaining targets still meet the minimum service level.
Details.errorCorrection: Waiting for a failure creates an avoidable outage, maximum does not define normal capacity, and interfaces on one host do not create independent failure domains.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A higher minimum costs more during quiet periods but can be required by availability and warm-up objectives.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A post-failure launch does not protect the service during launch and warm-up.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Maximum capacity does not preserve a serving baseline.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Multiple interfaces on one instance share its host and failure domain.

items.prompt: A scale-out alarm fires on every transient error spike, causing a fleet to grow while the dependency is unavailable. Which change is most important?
constraints: The error spike is caused by a shared downstream outage.
More instances do not repair the dependency.
The service needs an explicit degraded mode.

options.text: Separate demand and dependency-health signals, cap capacity, use backpressure or circuit behavior, and alert on the downstream outage rather than scaling blindly.
Remove the maximum capacity so the fleet can overcome any dependency outage by adding more callers.
Retry errors from every new instance immediately so the scale-out alarm receives more evidence.
Return successful empty responses so the error metric stops triggering the policy.

feedback.Reason: Scaling should respond to demand, not amplify a shared dependency failure that more instances cannot solve.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Capacity policies need signals that distinguish caller load from dependency error; bounded concurrency and explicit unavailable behavior prevent overload.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team raises a dependency incident, queues or rejects work according to contract, and avoids launching capacity that will only repeat failures.
Details.errorCorrection: Unbounded scale increases cost and pressure, retries amplify the outage, and fake success hides it.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A service may temporarily serve less work, but visible backpressure is safer than runaway capacity and silent corruption.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: More callers cannot repair a shared dependency outage and may worsen it.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Immediate retries add load while the dependency is already failing.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Fake success damages correctness and removes the signal without fixing availability.

items.prompt: Operators cannot explain why a fleet changed from 4 to 20 instances. What should the design provide?
constraints: Scaling actions are automated.
The organization needs cost and reliability auditability.
Signals, policy decisions, and lifecycle events are available.

options.text: Record scaling activities, policy alarms and metrics, desired and actual capacity, health events, and lifecycle transitions with correlation to the workload change.
Disable Auto Scaling logs because automation should not be inspected after it is configured.
Record only the final instance count and discard the signal that caused the change.
Ask operators to infer the reason from billing after the month closes.

feedback.Reason: Automated capacity must be observable so operators can verify whether the policy solved demand or amplified failure.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Activity history and metric correlation connect a capacity change to its alarm, policy, health, and lifecycle context.
Details.scenarioApplication: Operators can identify noisy signals, unexpected replacements, or downstream-driven scaling and tune the canonical policy.
Details.errorCorrection: Automation still needs evidence, a final count lacks causality, and billing is too delayed for operational diagnosis.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Detailed telemetry has cost and retention considerations, but unexplained capacity changes are a reliability and cost risk.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Unobserved automation cannot be safely diagnosed or improved.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: A final count does not explain the trigger or lifecycle path.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Billing cannot replace near-real-time operational evidence.

items.prompt: Which evidence best proves two tiers are independently scalable rather than merely placed in separate Auto Scaling groups?
constraints: The tiers share downstream dependencies.
The groups have separate policies.
The review must cover failure and capacity interaction.

options.text: Demonstrate separate demand signals, capacity bounds, deployment and health behavior, downstream protection, and load tests where one tier changes while the other remains stable.
Show only that the groups have different names in the console.
Show that both groups use the same instance type and policy so they behave identically.
Show that the two tiers share one broad IAM role and one security group.

feedback.Reason: Independent scaling is demonstrated by behavior and dependency contracts, not by naming or duplicated configuration.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: The test varies one workload and observes that only the appropriate capacity changes without violating shared quotas or service objectives.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team records request, queue, latency, connection, cost, and replacement outcomes for each tier.
Details.errorCorrection: Names do not create independence, identical policies couple behavior, and shared roles or groups weaken security ownership.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Independent groups need coordination at shared dependencies, so the evidence must include those boundaries too.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A label does not demonstrate independent demand or failure behavior.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Identical policy and capacity behavior can preserve coupling rather than prove independence.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Shared authority and network boundaries increase blast radius and do not prove scaling independence.
